lesson.title: Same Idea, Several Alphabets
lesson.summary: Surveys the main symbols used for the derivative, prime notation, Leibniz notation, and the d/dx operator, and confirms with a worked example that all three describe the identical function.
lesson.body:
Mathematics developed the derivative from more than one direction historically, geometry, physics, and pure algebra all arrived at the same limit, and each tradition left its own notation behind. As a result, a single derivative function can be written several different ways depending on context, and reading calculus fluently means recognizing that f prime of x, dy divided by dx, and d divided by dx of f(x) can all refer to the exact same object: the function that outputs the slope of the tangent, or equivalently the instantaneous rate of change, at whatever input you give it.

Lagrange's prime notation, f prime of x, treats the derivative as a new function built from f, with the prime mark signaling "the derivative of." Leibniz's notation, dy divided by dx, instead treats the derivative as a ratio of infinitesimally small changes, a small change in y divided by the small change in x that caused it, echoing the h in the difference quotient shrinking to nothing. A third common form, d divided by dx applied to an expression, is an instruction, "take the derivative of what follows with respect to x," useful when you want to differentiate an expression without first naming it y or f.

Take y = x cubed as a working example, whose derivative was found earlier by the limit definition to be 3 x squared. In prime notation this is written f prime of x = 3 x squared, or if the function is named y instead of f, simply y prime = 3 x squared. In Leibniz notation the same fact is dy divided by dx equals 3 x squared. As an instruction it reads d divided by dx of x cubed equals 3 x squared. All three statements are the identical mathematical fact expressed with different symbols.

Evaluating at a specific point also has parallel notations. Using the value x = 2, where the derivative was computed to be 12: prime notation writes f prime of 2 = 12, while Leibniz notation writes dy divided by dx, evaluated at x = 2, equals 12, usually drawn as a vertical bar after the expression with x = 2 written below it. Both statements say the tangent line to y = x cubed at the point where x = 2 has slope 12, nothing more and nothing less.

A fourth notation worth knowing by sight is Newton's, which places a dot above a variable to denote its derivative with respect to time: s-dot for the velocity ds divided by dt, and s-double-dot for the acceleration. Newton developed his version of calculus independently of Leibniz, largely to describe motion, which is why dot notation still shows up in physics texts describing rates of change over time, even though prime and Leibniz notation dominate in typical calculus courses.

Choosing between notations is mostly a matter of what makes later work easier. Prime notation is compact and convenient for naming higher derivatives quickly, while Leibniz notation makes the variables being differentiated explicit, which becomes valuable once multiple related quantities are changing together. The next two sections look at each notation in more depth, but the core message here is that a change of symbol is never a change of meaning: underneath every notation sits the same limit of a difference quotient.
